title: Reading from the right
explanation: Hebrew has 22 letters and is read from right to left. The first letter of a word is the one furthest right. The small dots and dashes around the letters show vowels. You will study those at the Vowel Springs. For now, look at the large letters.

workedExamples.note: Start at the right edge. ע (ayin) comes first, ר (resh) is next, and ב (bet) finishes on the left. Read in that order: e-rev.

title: What a word means here
explanation: A word card gives the usual meaning. The line around a word shows which meaning fits that place. Use Understand to say what a word means. The card will be hidden when you answer.

workedExamples.note: In Genesis 1:3 this word names a thing that comes to be: light. It is a noun here, so 'to shine' would be the wrong answer.

title: Five letters that change at the end
explanation: Five letters take a different shape when they end a word: כ becomes ך, מ becomes ם, נ becomes ן, פ becomes ף, and צ becomes ץ. It is the same letter in a different shape. Check the left end of the word, since that is where the word finishes.

workedExamples.note: Kaf ends this word, so it is written ך.
Mem ends this word, so it is written ם.
Nun ends this word, so it is written ן.
Pe ends this word, so it is written ף.
Tsade ends this word, so it is written ץ.

title: Reading the small marks
explanation: The dots and dashes around a letter are vowel signs, and most are read after the letter they sit under. This game's sound guide is a modern classroom reading of the pointing, not a claim about how the ancient language sounded. Five vowel qualities cover it. Read a for patah, a short line, and for qamats, a small T shape. Read e for segol, three dots, and for tsere, two dots side by side. Read i for hireq, one dot below, often with yod after it. Read o for holam, a dot above, often on a vav. Read u for shureq, a dot in the belly of a vav, and for qibbuts, three slanted dots. A word is split into syllables, each starting with one consonant, and each syllable has one vowel. Capital letters in a guide mark the stressed syllable, as in ya-MIM. The guide writes kh for het and for kaf with no dot, v for bet with no dot, q for qof and ts for tsade. Alef and ayin have no sound of their own here. A dot on the right arm of ש makes shin, sh, and a dot on the left arm makes sin, s.

workedExamples.note: Segol under ayin gives e, and segol under resh gives e. Ayin has no sound, and bet with no dot is v: E-rev. Two vowel signs, so two syllables.
A dot on top of the vav is holam-vav, read o. The vav carries the vowel and has no consonant sound here.
Patah under alef gives a, and alef itself has no sound. Yod is a consonant here, and hireq under it gives i: A-yin.
Qamats under yod gives a. Hireq with a yod after it gives i. The capitals in ya-MIM show that the stress falls on the last syllable.
Tsere, two dots side by side, gives e. Ayin has no sound, and final tsade is ts: ets.
A dot in the belly of the vav is shureq, read u. He is h, and the final alef is silent: hu.

title: Shewa and the words that attach
explanation: Two small dots stacked under a letter are a shewa. At the start of a word it is sounded very lightly, written e here. Closing a syllable, it is silent. Three short prepositions write as part of the next word: בְּ in, לְ to, כְּ like. The conjunction and prefixes behave the same way, so look for them before reading the word.

workedExamples.note: Shewa opens the word, so it is sounded: be-RIT.

workedExamples.translation: to, marked in the word for 'to me' forms
workedExamples.note: Here לְ is attached to קוֹל. It is a separate word in grammar, but it is written as one with its noun.

title: Joining marks and the other qamats
explanation: A maqqef is a short raised line that joins words, so they are read as one unit. Cantillation accents show stress and phrasing, and this game hides them in reading text but keeps them in the stored source. The qamats sign can also stand for a short o, called qamats qatan, in a closed unstressed syllable. So כָּל־ reads kol, even with the sign you learned as a.

workedExamples.note: This word is followed by a maqqef and has no stress of its own, so its qamats is short: kol.

title: The dot inside a letter
explanation: A dot inside a letter is a dagesh. In six letters, בגדכפת, it can mark a hard sound: bet b, kaf k, pe p. In many letters it marks doubling, even when the modern reading doesn't double the sound. A dot in final he is a mappiq: it shows that the he is a real consonant, not a silent vowel letter. With no dot, a final he is silent. Don't mix up these jobs: where the dot sits and which letter carries it tell you which one you have.

workedExamples.note: The word starts with a dagesh in bet, so it reads b, not v.
Lamed isn't one of the six letters, so its dot marks doubling: EL-leh.

title: The article hides in the word
explanation: Hebrew has no separate word for the. The article is usually הַ plus a dagesh in the next letter. There is no word for a, so a noun with no article can be read with a. The word's own form doesn't change, but the pointing around the join does. In the same way, a preposition absorbs the article: בַּ means in the.

workedExamples.note: He with patah is the article, and the dagesh goes in shin.
The article's he disappears. Its patah moves under the preposition, and the dagesh stays.

title: Letters that won't double
explanation: The gutturals א ה ח ע, along with ר, resist doubling, so they can't take a dagesh. When the article meets one, the patah usually lengthens to qamats or the vowel changes: הָאוֹר, הָעִיר. Gutturals also prefer a-class vowels and take composite shewas like hataf patah or hataf segol instead of a plain vocal shewa. Letters such as alef and he can also fall silent at the end of a syllable, and then they simply stop being pronounced.

workedExamples.note: Alef can't double, so the article has qamats and no dagesh follows.
Alef takes hataf patah, a composite shewa, here shown in הָאֲדָמָה.

title: Gender and number
explanation: Every Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine. Masculine plurals usually end in ִים, and feminine plurals usually end in וֹת. Feminine singulars often end in ָה or ת. These are only patterns: a few nouns break them, and gender comes from the dictionary, not the ending. A singular noun can also be collective, naming a whole group: עוֹף, birds. Some nouns are plural or dual in form with a singular meaning: מַיִם, שָׁמַיִם, פָּנִים.

workedExamples.note: The ending ִים marks the plural of a masculine noun. The first vowel changes too.
This feminine noun takes ִים anyway. The ending doesn't decide the gender.

title: Sentences with no verb, and the waw
explanation: Hebrew often makes a statement with no verb "to be": just two items next to each other, and English supplies is or was. The conjunction and is a prefix, usually וְ. Before most letters with a shewa, or before ב, מ, פ, it becomes וּ. Before a stressed syllable in a pair it can be וָ.

workedExamples.translation: I, in a clause with no verb
workedExamples.note: The clause is עֵירֹם אָנֹכִי: naked, I. English needs 'I am naked', but Hebrew has no verb.
Before bet, the waw turns into וּ, shureq, and it is read u.
In a close pair before a stressed syllable, the waw takes qamats.

title: Noun patterns and the preposition from
explanation: Many common nouns have the stress on the first syllable and two segols, like מֶלֶךְ and אֶרֶץ. They are called segholates. With a guttural the pattern shifts: נַעַר has patahs. The preposition מִן means from. It can stand alone or attach to the next word: then its nun disappears and doubles the next letter, as מִבַּיִת. In comparisons, it also means than: this is greater from that.

workedExamples.note: Stress on the first syllable, with two segols: the segholate pattern.
Nun has assimilated: the dagesh in bet marks where it went.
Before the article here, it stands alone with a maqqef.

title: Describing and comparing
explanation: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number. When it describes the noun, it follows, and if the noun has the article, so does the adjective: הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל. When it says something about the noun, it has no article and usually stands first: טוֹב. Hebrew has no ending for comparative: it uses מִן, so good from means better than.

workedExamples.note: The noun has the article, so its adjective does too: the great light.
Here it says something about the subject, with no article.

title: The perfect tense
explanation: A verb is listed by its Qal perfect third person masculine singular, like שָׁמַר, he kept. The perfect adds endings to mark who: ָה she, תָּ you, תִּי I, וּ they. This form is often called qatal. It often describes a completed event, so English usually uses a past, but not always: with a verb like know it can be present. A tense label isn't a full account of what the form does.

workedExamples.note: The stem שמע plus the ending תִּי marks first person.
The stem לקח plus the ending תָּ marks you, masculine singular.
English uses a present here. The perfect with this verb describes a state.

title: Marking the object
explanation: In a verbal clause the verb often comes first, then the subject, then the object. A definite direct object is marked with אֵת, written אֶת־ before a maqqef. This marker isn't a word in English, and it isn't the same as אֵת, with. An indefinite object has no marker. The verb agrees with its subject in gender and number. Word order can vary, so read the endings, not just the positions.

workedExamples.note: The clause is בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם: verb, subject, then the marked object.
The word כִּי opens a clause after a verb of seeing.

title: I, you, he, this, these
explanation: Independent pronouns stand as subjects: אֲנִי or אָנֹכִי I, אַתָּה you, הוּא he, הִוא she, הֵם or הֵמָּה they. A perfect verb already has its person in its ending, so an added pronoun often adds emphasis. Demonstratives point: זֶה this, masculine; זֹאת this, feminine; אֵלֶּה these. Like adjectives, when they describe a noun they follow it and match its article.

workedExamples.note: It refers back to a masculine noun, the river, so English says it.
It points to the woman, so the feminine form is used.
A single form covers masculine and feminine plurals.

title: The construct bridge
explanation: Two nouns placed together can mean X of Y. The first is in the construct state: it loses its stress, and often its vowels shorten or its ending changes. The article goes only on the last noun, and that makes the whole chain definite: בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ is the house of the king. Feminine ָה changes to ַת, and plural ִים changes to ֵי.

workedExamples.note: The chain is שֵׁם הָאֶחָד: name of the first. The first noun has no article, and the chain is definite because of the second.
The plural noun פָּנִים becomes פְּנֵי: its ending ִים changes to ֵי.
בַּיִת shortens to בֵּית in the construct.

title: Suffixes on prepositions
explanation: Pronoun endings attach to prepositions: to me, with you, from it. The endings repeat across the language: ִי my or me, ךָ your, וֹ his, הּ her, ם their. The stem may change, as with אִתּ- for אֵת with, or עִמּ- for עִם. Some prepositions take the plural-looking set: אֵלַי, עָלָיו. It doesn't mean several: the shape comes with the preposition.

workedExamples.note: עִם doubles its mem before the ending, and הּ marks her.
The ending ַי marks me. Its yod comes from this preposition's plural-looking shape.
The ending ָיו marks him, again with the plural-looking shape.

title: There is, and verbs ending in alef
explanation: יֵשׁ says something exists, and אַיִן says it doesn't. Before another word it is usually אֵין. Withלְ they say who has it, as Hebrew has no verb for have. Short particles like גַּם also, עוֹד again, הִנֵּה look and כֵּן so belong here too, adding emphasis to clauses. When a verb's root ends in alef, the alef often falls silent and the vowel before it lengthens: מָצָאתִי, not a patah. The word אֲשֶׁר links a clause to a noun: it covers who, which and that, and it doesn't change form.

workedExamples.note: The clause is יֵשׁ חֲמִשִּׁים: there are fifty.
The root ends in alef, which is silent here, and the vowel before it is qamats.
It links the clause back to the waters.

title: My, your, his, on singular nouns
explanation: A noun takes the same family of endings to show who owns it: ִי my, ךָ your, וֹ his, הּ her, ם or ָם their. The noun appears in its construct-like stem before the ending, so it can shorten: דָּבָר but דְּבָרוֹ. Some nouns change more: בַּיִת becomes בֵּית-, and פֶּה becomes פִּי-. A first segol can also become patah: נֶפֶשׁ, נַפְשִׁי my soul. Family words like אָח add an extra yod before the ending: אָחִיו his brother. A noun with a suffix is definite and takes no article.

workedExamples.note: The noun plus ִי means my.
שֵׁם shortens to שְׁמ- before וֹ.
The stem of אָחוֹת changes before the ending ִי.

title: Suffixes on plural nouns
explanation: Plural nouns take a set of endings with a yod: ַי my, ֶיךָ your, ָיו his, ֶיהָ her. The yod here isn't part of the noun, and it often isn't pronounced: it marks the plural. So ָיו and וֹ both mean his, but one is on many things and one is on one. Dual nouns take the same plural set, as with עֵינַיִם.

workedExamples.note: פָּנִים is plural in form, so it takes the plural set ָיו.
The dual noun takes the plural set, and כֶם marks you, plural.

title: The participle
explanation: The Qal active participle has holam, then tsere: שֹׁמֵר, one keeping. It works like an adjective and a verb together. It takes noun endings for gender and number. With the article it means the one who does: הַהֹלֵךְ, the one going. On its own it often describes ongoing action, so English needs -ing.

workedExamples.note: Holam on the first letter and tsere on the second mark the Qal participle.
The same pattern. The patah under ayin is furtive and read before it.

title: The imperfect
explanation: The imperfect adds prefixes as well as endings: יִ he, תִּ you or she, אֶ I, נִ we. Plurals add וּ. This form is often called yiqtol. It often points to future, repeated or possible action, so English may use will, would or may. A ָה added to a place name or a noun marks direction, called directive he: toward. It is unstressed and isn't a feminine ending.

workedExamples.note: The prefix תִּ marks you, and the stem has holam.
The context is repeated past action, not future: mist used to rise.
The ending ָה on שָׁם marks direction: toward there.

title: Telling a story with waw
explanation: Biblical stories move forward with a special verb form: waw with patah, plus a doubled prefix, then an imperfect-looking verb: וַיִּקְרָא, and he called. This is the waw consecutive or wayyiqtol. It carries a past story forward, one event after another. The verb הָיָה often appears as וַיְהִי to move time forward: and it came to pass. With the prefix alef of I, the waw has qamats, since alef can't double: וָאֹכֵל, and I ate. Don't translate it as a dictionary infinitive.

workedExamples.note: Waw with patah, then a dagesh in the prefix yod: the sign of the narrative form.
This form of הָיָה often pushes time forward. Yod with shewa can't take a dagesh, so none appears.
The first narrative form you'll see most often.

title: State verbs and questions
explanation: Some verbs describe a state, not an action, and their perfect often has tsere or holam in the second syllable: מָלֵא be full, יָרֵא fear, יָכֹל be able. English can use the present for their perfect. Questions can open with הֲ, or with a question word such as מִי who, מָה what. Conditions use אִם, if. A clause can also be a question with no marker at all, from context.

workedExamples.note: Tsere in the second syllable marks this stative.
A question word opens the clause.
The he with hataf patah on יֵשׁ makes a yes-or-no question.

title: Commands and wishes
explanation: Hebrew has three forms for expressing will. The imperative commands you: it looks like the imperfect without its prefix. The jussive wishes a third person: יְהִי, let there be. The cohortative wishes first person, often with an ending ָה: let me, let us. Negative wishes and commands use אַל, not לֹא. The particle נָא softens a request.

workedExamples.note: A jussive, not a past tense.
A plural imperative, addressed to the creatures.
The negative that goes with wishes.

title: Interrupting the story, and passive participles
explanation: When waw attaches to a word that isn't a verb, it breaks the narrative chain. It often gives background or sets up a contrast: וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה, now the earth was. Compare וַיִּקְרָא, which moves the story on. The Qal passive participle has a shureq in the second syllable, for example אָרוּר, cursed: done to, not doing. Words at a pause in a verse can have longer vowels: לָיְלָה for לַיְלָה.

workedExamples.note: Waw on a noun gives background: the story pauses to describe the scene.
Qamats here marks the verse's pause. The word is otherwise לַיְלָה.
Shureq in the second syllable marks the passive participle, and it agrees with the ground, a feminine noun.

title: Infinitives
explanation: The infinitive construct is a verbal noun, usually with לְ meaning to: לִשְׁמֹר, to keep. With בְּ or כְּ it marks when: while doing. It can take a suffix for the subject. The infinitive absolute stands alone, usually before a finite verb from the same root, and it adds emphasis: מוֹת תָּמוּת, you will surely die.

workedExamples.note: The preposition plus an infinitive construct gives a purpose. Patah appears before the guttural.
An absolute before the finite verb: surely die.

title: Objects on the verb
explanation: A verb can carry its object as an ending: him, her, them, me. Instead of the separate אֹתוֹ, Hebrew may write the object on the verb. The vowels of the verb shift to make room, so you need to look through to the root. These endings are close to noun suffixes but work as objects, not owners.

workedExamples.note: The verb בָּרָא plus ָם, them, with its first vowel shortened.
A narrative verb can take an object suffix too.

title: Counting
explanation: אֶחָד one and שְׁנַיִם two agree with their noun in gender. Numbers three to ten show reversed gender: the form with ָה goes with masculine nouns, and the short form goes with feminine nouns. שָׁנָה year is feminine, so Genesis says חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים. Above ten a noun can stay singular: מְאַת שָׁנָה, a hundred year. Don't read that as a mistake.

workedExamples.note: A short form, with a feminine noun: five years.
The form ending in ָה, used with a masculine count.
A construct of מֵאָה before שָׁנָה, singular.

title: The Niphal
explanation: Stems are patterns that change how a root works, and they don't map to one fixed English meaning. The Niphal often gives a passive or reflexive sense, and some verbs simply use it for their normal meaning. Its perfect has a prefix נִ: נִשְׁמַר. In its imperfect the nun assimilates, leaving a dagesh in the first root letter: תִּקָּבֵר.

workedExamples.note: Prefix נִ marks the Niphal perfect. This verb's ordinary meaning uses the Niphal, with no passive sense.
The nun has assimilated into qof, leaving a dagesh, and the sense is passive.

title: The Piel and Pual
explanation: The Piel doubles the middle root letter. Its perfect has hireq, then tsere or segol: דִּבֶּר. Its imperfect and narrative forms have shewa under the prefix: וַיְדַבֵּר. It often marks an intensive or causative sense, but many verbs simply live here: דָבַר speak, בָּרַךְ bless, צָוָה command. A guttural or resh in the middle can't double, so the vowel lengthens: בֵּרַךְ. Its participle has prefix מְ: מְרַחֶפֶת, hovering. The Pual is its passive partner, with a u-vowel first. Grammars read a few such forms, like לֻקַּח and יֻלַּד, as an old Qal passive instead. OSHB, the annotation this game cites, tags them Pual, so a question about OSHB's label has that answer.

workedExamples.note: A dagesh in bet doubles the middle root letter.
Shewa under the prefix yod marks the Piel. Resh can't double.
A dagesh in the vav doubles it, and the hireq first marks the perfect.
Pual: a u-vowel first, and a doubled middle letter. It is the passive partner of the Piel.

title: The Hithpael
explanation: The Hithpael adds a prefix הִתְ, doubles the middle letter, and often gives a reflexive or iterative sense: to act on oneself. When the first root letter is a sibilant like ש, the tav swaps places with it. The common verb for bowing, וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ, is unusual: OSHB tags narrative forms as Hithpael and others in a related Hishtaphel pattern, and grammars analyse its root differently. The game flags this rather than picking one account.

workedExamples.note: Look for tav after the shin: it has swapped places.
Prefix הִתְ and a doubled middle letter, the regular Hithpael shape.

title: The Hiphil and Hophal
explanation: The Hiphil often means to cause something: to make go out is to bring out. Its perfect has prefix הִ and usually a long i in the second syllable: הִגִּיד. Its narrative form has patah under the prefix: וַיַּבְדֵּל. Its participle has prefix מַ: מַבְדִּיל, one separating. Some verbs use it for a basic meaning, such as tell. The Hophal is its passive partner, with an o or u vowel in the prefix, and is rare.

workedExamples.note: A patah under the prefix, and tsere in the second syllable of this short narrative form.
Qal יָצָא is go out, and Hiphil is bring out.
Prefix הִ and a long i. The first root letter nun has assimilated.
Hophal: a u-vowel on the prefix, the passive partner of the Hiphil.

title: Parsing a verb, step by step
explanation: To parse a verb, work in order. First strip any waw and any object suffix. Find the prefix or ending to get person, gender and number. Use the vowel under the prefix and any doubling to find the stem. Then ask for the conjugation: perfect, imperfect, narrative, imperative, participle or infinitive. Several forms can look alike, so the sentence has the last word.

workedExamples.note: Waw with patah and a dagesh in yod: narrative. Prefix yod with no ending: he. Hireq under the prefix and no doubled root letter: Qal. The shewa closes a syllable, so the dagesh in dalet only keeps it hard.

title: Gutturals in verbs
explanation: A guttural first root letter takes composite shewa instead of plain shewa, and prefers a-class vowels: יַעֲלֶה, not a plain shewa. A guttural last letter has an a-vowel before it where other verbs have another vowel, or takes a furtive patah: יֹדֵעַ. These changes follow the guttural rules you learned at the Springs, not new verb rules.

workedExamples.note: Ayin as the first root letter takes hataf patah.
Alef as the last root letter is silent, and the vowel before it lengthens.

title: Verbs that lose a nun
explanation: When a root's first letter is nun, the nun often assimilates: it disappears and leaves a dagesh in the next letter. So וַיִּתֵּן comes from נתן. The same happens to לקח, whose lamed behaves like a nun in this way: וַיִּקַּח. When you see a dagesh after the prefix with no visible first letter, suspect a missing nun. A letter carrying a shewa can drop that dagesh, so its absence doesn't rule out a missing nun.

workedExamples.note: The dagesh in tav marks the first nun. The last nun remains.
The first nun of נשא is gone, but this form has no dagesh to mark it, as sin carries a shewa. The dagesh you can see is the narrative one, in prefix yod.

title: Verbs that begin with yod
explanation: Many verbs listed with first letter yod lose it in the imperfect and narrative forms, and the prefix has tsere: וַיֵּשֶׁב, וַיֵּרֶד. The original letter in many of them was waw, and it reappears in the Hiphil: וַיּוֹלֶד, וַתּוֹצֵא. The verb הָלַךְ behaves like this group in the imperfect. So when you see tsere under the prefix and two visible letters, think I-yod.

workedExamples.note: The yod of יָשַׁב is gone, and tsere is under the prefix.
In the Hiphil, a vav shows up in the old first-letter position.

title: Verbs that end in he, and double trouble
explanation: In verbs whose citation form ends in ה, that he is only a vowel letter. Before endings it changes or drops: עָשִׂית, רָאִיתִי. In a narrative form the end can drop altogether, which is why וַיַּעַשׂ, וַיַּרְא and וַיְהִי look so short. Some verbs are weak in two ways at once: הָיָה and חָיָה both have a guttural-like first letter and a final he.

workedExamples.note: The final he is gone. Only עשׂ remains after the prefix.
Before the ending, he turns into a yod glide.
A short form from חָיָה: weak at two points.

title: Hollow verbs (supplement)
explanation: This lesson is a supplement: the checked table of contents stops at chapter 37 and doesn't confirm where these verbs are treated. A hollow verb has a vowel in its middle: קוּם, שׁוּב, מוּת, and בּוֹא is similar. The dictionary uses a form with vav, but in the perfect that vav disappears, so only two letters show: שָׁב, בָּא. Geminate verbs, where the last two root letters match, also shrink, and can be read the same way.

workedExamples.note: Two letters and qamats: the perfect of שׁוּב.
A qamats in the prefix and no vav. This narrative form is from קוּם.

title: Reading a whole clause
explanation: Now you read full lines. Find the verb first. Then find its subject and any object marked by אֶת. Use prepositions to see how the other nouns connect. Keep word meanings loose until the clause settles them. You may see words you haven't captured: every gloss is on hand, because the goal is reading, not memorizing.

workedExamples.note: The preposition בְּ with a noun sets the time before the verb arrives.
The verb comes next, and it is a Qal perfect, third person masculine singular.

title: Chains and pauses, revisited
explanation: This revisits narrative sequence and the disjunctive waw, now across several verses. A chain of waw-narrative forms moves events along. A waw on a non-verb stops the chain to set a scene. Genesis 1:2 is one long scene-setter, and Genesis 1:3 starts the chain. Notice how a perfect, הָיְתָה, sits inside the background clause.

workedExamples.note: Waw on a noun means background.
The chain starts here and moves the story on.

title: Genesis 1:1-5
explanation: The restored archive's first page is Genesis 1:1-5, taken from the Westminster Leningrad Codex. Every token keeps its source mark order, and the reading text hides only the accents. Translations are original to this game and offer one reading among honest options. For example, רוּחַ can be wind or spirit, and בְּרֵאשִׁית has a long-debated syntax, so the game doesn't pretend either is settled.

workedExamples.note: A jussive form: God's word is a wish that becomes fact.
Hebrew says day one, a cardinal where English expects first.
